definition: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity.
details: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity. It is a primary tool in computational complexity theory to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows.

explainer.lead: Big-O notation describes how a function’s cost grows as its input becomes very large or approaches a particular value. In computing, it helps compare algorithms by how their running time or memory needs scale, without tying the answer to a particular machine.

tiers.eli5: Imagine handing out invitations to a party. If each extra guest means one more envelope, the work grows steadily; if every guest must be compared with every other guest, the work grows much faster. Big-O is a short way to describe that growth pattern while ignoring small fixed chores like finding your pen.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use Big-O to compare algorithms and data structures as input size n grows, usually counting time or extra space. An O(n) scan and an O(n^2) nested comparison can behave very differently at scale, but the notation hides constant factors and lower-order costs. Use measurements on realistic inputs alongside asymptotic analysis, and do not assume Big-O specifies worst-case, average-case, or exact running time by itself.
tiers.paperLevel: For growth at infinity, f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants M and n0 such that |f(n)| <= M|g(n)| for all n >= n0. The notation gives an asymptotic upper bound and can also describe limiting behavior near a particular argument value. It suppresses constant factors and lower-order terms, so it does not determine exact machine time, space usage for a fixed input, or the input distribution.

explainer.example: If an algorithm compares every pair among n items, it makes n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which equals 0.5n^2 - 0.5n. Its comparison count is O(n^2), because the squared term dominates as n grows; at n = 100 it makes 4,950 comparisons, while at n = 1,000 it makes 499,500.

usedIn.detail: Compares candidate approaches before choosing one for large inputs.

usedIn.name: Software performance analysis
usedIn.detail: Helps reason about how running time or memory use may scale as workloads increase.

explainer.intuition: Big-O focuses on the long-term shape of growth rather than the exact cost of one run. It keeps the part of a function that dominates at the limit and hides constant factors and smaller terms.
howItWorks: Choose an input measure, such as the number of items n.
Express running time or space use as a function of n.
Consider behavior as n grows toward infinity, or toward the chosen limiting value.
Keep the dominant growth term and omit constant factors and lower-order terms.
Use the resulting class to compare how different algorithms scale.
explainer.whyItMatters: Big-O makes algorithm growth comparable across different machines and implementations. It can reveal when an approach that works well on small inputs may become impractical as the input grows.
misconceptions: Big-O is not an exact running-time formula or a duration in seconds.
Writing O(n) does not, by itself, specify worst-case or average-case behavior.
A better Big-O class does not guarantee faster execution for every input size.
